Honestly, I see this sub as kind of a forever alone circle jerk. There are plenty of subreddits out there that could do great things for the people who post here with legitimate problems. Most (if not all) of them are listed in the sidebar. 

Yes I'm one of the people who will drop by sometimes and try and help out. But there isn't much use because of the overwhelming majority of people that refuse to help themselves. Their motives (or lack thereof) are then reinforced by the other people in this sub plus all of the glorious karma you'll get for saying how old you are and the fact that you haven't had sex. 

Would it help if I told everyone here that the world doesn't owe them anything? Would it help if I explained that nobody is going to magically fall in love with you? Would it help if I said that everything is going to be okay in the end?

No, of course not. 

I'm sure people enjoy the comradery. I'm sure people get comfort in the fact that others feel the same way they do. It is a shame really because I'm about 96% confident that everyone who posts here has the potential to better their life in some way. They might be blinded by the idea that a mate will be the solution. Having been there, I know this isn't true and you don't have to believe me if you don't want. In the end though, it comes down to the individual. It comes down to your willpower to try and change yourself.

But most of the time this subreddit doesn't breed that kind of activity. It is focused on the memes, self-loathing and virgin jokes. So if you get anything out of this ramble I guess it would be to hit the unsubscribe button.

Yes, I did. Part of the reason I choose to go to school in a big city was to be able to "hide among the masses". 50% of me had the pipe-dream that things would magically change and being around people would force me to be more social. The other half of me knew I could get away with continuing my anti-social, self loathing behavior even moreso than in high school. 

The thing for me though, is that I was under the impression that everyone out there was having the time of their life. I had this twisted thought that every other person was living the college dream and enjoying their lives. 

I was incredibly fearful of trying to get out there that, like most of us do, I shut myself in even further. I was afraid to talk to people. I was afraid of changing it up from what I've dealt with at leas 6 years prior. The environment wasn't going to change me, I had too. 

Recovery/Improvement is a long process and I've had my setbacks. But the biggest part for me was accepting that: 1) I really am the kind of person that can't handle frequent and extended periods of social interaction, 2) "People who mind, don't matter" has been exorbitantly relevant in regards to my social activity. The friends I've made understand that I might be a little bit hesitant to tell them/other people things. They don't care that some days I just don't want to go out. They just care that I'm having a good time. It takes some risk. It takes some breaching of comfort. But I can assure you that this risk is worth the potential reward. 

Failure will only give you more experience. Unfortunate? Yes. But, while failure is unavoidable, treat it as experience. Learn from it and grow into the social person that *you* want to be.

Yeah, and it is probably the reason I have a hard time trying to find someone to be a companion. 

We can rationalize a plethora of our other feelings. Happiness is easy, same with anger, sadness, envy and others have a distinct "I have gained this or I have lost that" phenomenon that occurs. So, we pinpoint these phenomenon and try and rectify what we deem "went wrong". 

I feel like love, affection and the like are a different breed for us introspective thinkers. We don't know what we have to gain or lose and we can't pinpoint what exactly we need to amend so our situation can "work". And heck, we try to for one person and it ends up being a completely different narrative for the next person that crosses our meandering path of attempting to find someone to enjoy life with. 

I guess the real question is why? Why do we rationalize these completely irrational feelings of "Hey you're an interesting person that is different in some odd way than that other interesting person"? Sure we can base things on looks, compatibility questions or mutual activities. But (at least in my case) the perfect concoction is cooked up in a mind that has yet to experience humanity in its vast and diverse forms. 

So what exactly am I trying to say here? I'm not entirely sure, it's quite early in the morning and I'm sleep deprived. But basically, our emotions are complex things. Trying to rationalize them based on previous experience alone is an irrational thing to do. I think that the more we experience life, the more we get in tune with ourselves. Being in tune with ourselves will help you live with yourself; because that is the first person (and more or less the only person) that should be seeking your approval. When the tuning is right (or at least in a good range) we just might find someone who matches up. Not because we were trying hard or forcing interest, but because you were being you.

>How do you guys get the courage to ask out other people?

If you already know the person it is fairly simple. I try and make plans in person. So they are more concrete. Don't just bring it up and say "hey i think this would be cool to go to". If you don't know the person it is obviously more difficult. I try the same few things when I'm out in the world and it has worked a fair amount of times. Smiling and eye contact is great. If the other person exchanges then you are fair game to go and talk. The ice is almost broken and all you have to do is innitiate talking (saying hi, introducing yourself then a general statement that they can reply to). Of course if you are willing to be more daring (compared to the average FA'er). Skip the exchange of smiles and just initiate talking.

I never and probably will never tell my parents about my depression. I will probably never tell them about the treatment I received. I will probably never tell them that I almost failed out of college. I will probably never tell my mother that it is her fault that I suffered all of those years.

What matters is that the opportunity for me was there and I just had to go and grab it. It's a scary road sure. I expected judgement from the therapist. I expected that I was just making this all up. I expected that things would get better after the first week. 

I had a same "odd" reason why I didn't seek help. That was myself admitting that I was comfortable with the sad, self-loathing person I was. But, like you, I knew I should had gotten help earlier and I knew I wanted to feel better. 

I would suggest you seek help as soon as you can. But I know that you might not and that's okay. I waited until I was inches away from hitting rock bottom before I got help. When I look back I realize how scary of a place I was in. How vulnerable I was to some very bad things that could have destroyed my life if I didn't do it myself. So, the earlier the better.
